description: For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to develop creative solutions for astronaut health monitoring during space missions. We welcome passionate teammates interested in software development, coding, AI/ML, data analysis, design, presentation and space science. Let's innovate together for a healthier future in space!
summary:
Breath First is a web-based health and life-support monitoring console that lets a space crew check their own health and their spacecraft's environment without waiting for Earth. It maps all 17 NASA Human Research Program risks to a self-checkable indicator, reads every indicator from three redundant sensors (the median wins; disagreement raises a sensor-fault alert), and gives plain-language actions when a value drifts toward a threshold, including trend warnings that estimate the minutes left before a limit is reached.
The challenge asks for software that helps astronauts monitor their health on space missions. Breath First answers it with a priority-ordered dashboard (oxygen, CO₂ and cabin pressure first), a health score and weekly vitals for each astronaut, a radiation dose budget with a cited neutron share, a replay mode for drills, an energy-efficient e-ink view, and a one-page handoff report for ground teams.
It matters because communication slows with distance: a message to Mars can take 4 to 24 minutes each way. Crews need tools that let them act now, trust their data, and keep Earth in the loop when it can catch up.
details:
What it does

Breath First is a browser-based health and life-support console for astronaut crews. It ranks every indicator by how quickly it could hurt the crew: oxygen, CO₂ and cabin pressure come first, then reserves (oxygen tank, water), then comfort and radiation, then each astronaut's vitals. Each of the 17 risks in NASA's Human Research Program is linked to a body region, an indicator, normal/caution/critical levels, self-check steps and a clear action, including when to call the ground.

How it works

  • Redundancy: every indicator is read by three sensors and the median wins. A drifting sensor is outvoted and logged; if all three disagree, the median is still shown but a sensor-fault alert is raised.
  • Home shows the crew at a glance and the priority ladder. Crew gives a health score and weekly vitals for each astronaut. Charts shows the radiation dose budget (with the Canadian Space Agency figure that neutrons make up about 30% of ISS radiation) and medicine stock as pie and donut charts. Sensors shows which sensors can still be trusted.
  • Trend warnings estimate how many minutes remain before a value reaches its limit, so the crew can act before the alarm.
  • Alerts are acknowledged, not deleted, so there is a full audit trail.
  • Replay mode runs drill scenarios (for example Hypoxia Onset) at adjustable speed for training.
  • Designed for distance: a comms-delay mode simulates Moon or Mars latency (4 to 24 minutes each way), a one-page handoff report summarises a shift for the ground team, and a low-power e-ink view shows the essentials using very little energy.
  • Safety by design: pressure logic only alarms and guides repressurisation; it never vents on its own.

Benefits and impact

Crews far from Earth cannot wait for mission control. Breath First helps them notice problems early, trust their readings, focus on the alert that matters most instead of a wall of alarms, and keep the ground informed when the link catches up. The same approach could support remote and isolated workplaces on Earth.

Tools and technologies

Plain HTML, vanilla JavaScript, Bootstrap and Chart.js on the front end, with a lightweight backend serving a REST API. There is no build step and no Docker, so it runs in any modern browser on Windows, macOS or Linux. Sensor readings are simulated for the demo. AI coding assistants helped with parts of the code and documentation, and this is disclosed in the README.

What makes it creative

Instead of a dashboard that treats every number equally, Breath First puts air first and builds redundancy into every reading. The e-ink view and the handoff report are designed specifically for long missions with limited power and delayed communication.

What we considered

Oxygen matters more than water; sensors fail and drift; alarm fatigue hides real emergencies; energy is limited; and communication delays grow with distance. Next steps are a colour e-ink crew display and connecting real sensors.
